info.title: gocommerce
info.description:
A small, composable commerce engine for Go.

Money is always an integer count of the currency's minor unit plus its code — never a float, never a formatted string. The number of decimal places belongs to the currency (USD has 2, JPY has 0, KWD has 3) and formatting belongs to the client.

Every response is `{"data": ...}` or `{"error": {"code", "message"}}`. Every collection paginates.

Guest checkout is permanent: a shopper needs a cart token and an email, never an account.

get.description: Reports that the process is running. Touches no dependency, so a database hiccup never causes an orchestrator to restart a healthy process.
Reports that this process can serve traffic, which requires the database to answer.
The contract this build serves, including paths contributed by installed modules.
Only active products are visible. A draft or archived product is reported as not found rather than forbidden, because its existence is not a shopper's business.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Free-text match on title and description.

parameters.name: attr
parameters.description: Filter by a category attribute's recorded value, as `handle:value` — for example `attr=bag-case-material:Canvas`. Repeat the parameter to add more. Several values of the SAME handle widen the result (canvas OR leather, because a shopper who ticks both wants either); different handles narrow it (canvas AND black, because they describe one item). Only the first colon separates, so `color:Black:ish` is the value "Black:ish". Matching is exact, not a substring. An entry with no colon, no handle or no value is ignored rather than refused, so a truncated URL narrows to everything or to nothing instead of taking the listing away. The values are the ones stored under `metadata.category` by the category's own field list.

parameters.name: channel
parameters.description: Which storefront is asking. Absent takes the default channel; a store with no channels reads the whole catalogue, exactly as before channels existed. An unknown or inactive code is refused with a 400 rather than quietly served the default — a typo in a storefront's configuration should fail at its first request, not sell the wrong catalogue for a week.

get.summary: Get an active product by slug
Get a product by one of its variant SKUs
get.description: SKU is the catalog's stable key for import and export, which makes it the natural handle for a storefront deep link too.

get.summary: List the collections a storefront should show
get.description: Only collections holding at least one active product are listed. A collection that is empty, or that holds nothing but drafts, is a work in progress, and linking to it would produce an empty page.

200.description: A page of collections, in curation order.

get.summary: Get a collection and the active products in it
get.description: `meta` describes the embedded products: the collection itself is a single record, and the only thing on this response a client can page through is what is in it. Products come back in the order they were curated.

200.description: The collection with a page of its active products.

get.description: Variants are their own collection rather than a sub-path of a product: `/api/products/{id}/variants` would collide with the slug and sku lookups.

post.description: Returns the cart id, which is an unguessable token. Possessing it is the authorisation — there is no account, and there never has to be.

channel.description: Which storefront opened the basket. The `X-Channel` header says the same thing store-wide; the body wins when both are present. Fixed at creation, because it is what every line's price is resolved against — a basket that changed storefront halfway would hold lines priced on two and no honest way to say which total is right.

parameters.name: X-Channel
parameters.description: The storefront, for clients that set it once rather than per request.

post.summary: Add a variant to the cart
post.description: Adding records the price now. Checkout is what makes a price authoritative, and it refuses rather than silently repricing.

patch.description: A quantity of zero removes the line, which is what a stepper stepping down to nothing means.

put.summary: Set the shopper's email on a cart
put.description: The address an abandoned-cart flow reaches the shopper on. A shopper types it into the checkout form mid-session, before checkout exists to capture it, and this is where it is recorded. An empty string clears it, which is the shopper's own way to withdraw the address. Like every cart mutation it extends the cart's TTL, and it revives a cart the sweeper has already marked `abandoned`.

email.description: An empty string clears the address.

get.summary: List the payment methods this store accepts

200.description: Installed payment codes, and the same list with display names.

methods.description: The same set as `payment_methods`, in the same order, with the name each provider gives itself — the string to put beside a radio button. Both shapes exist on purpose and neither replaces the other: `payment_methods` is the array of codes every storefront already reads, and a future tidy-up that collapses them breaks those readers to save a key.

code.description: What the API speaks: the code in the checkout URL.

name.description: The label to show a person. Falls back to the code when the provider offers no name, which is the same answer GET /api/admin/settings gives for the same provider.

post.summary: Check out with a payment method
post.description:
Validates the cart, reserves inventory and creates the order in one transaction, then starts payment outside it — a gateway having a slow day must not become the store having a slow day.

If a line's price changed, its product went inactive, or stock ran out, the whole checkout is refused with 409 and per-line detail; the cart is refreshed to current prices so the shopper can confirm again.

Send an `Idempotency-Key` header. The same key replays the original result instead of creating a second order; if the first attempt created the order but payment initiation failed, a retry resumes payment on that same order.

parameters.name: code
parameters.description: A payment method code, such as `cod`.

201.description: The order, and what the client must do to pay.

409.description: The cart is no longer valid at these prices.

error.message: the cart is no longer valid at these prices

post.description: A core-owned route that hands the raw request body to the payment module, so a gateway gets a documented callback URL without the module mounting anything itself. Signature verification is the module's job.

get.description: Guest checkout means there is no account to log into, so the order's access token — returned once at checkout — is the credential. A wrong token is reported as not found, so this cannot be used to discover which order numbers exist.

Newest first, which is what "select existing" wants: the file you just uploaded is usually the one you want. Every filter narrows in the store, so a page of results is a page of the whole library rather than of what a client already holds.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Case-insensitive substring of the filename, the alt text or the URL. A substring rather than full text, because a library is names, not prose.

parameters.name: usage
parameters.description: `used` is media at least one product displays; `unused` is the orphans, which is the reason the filter exists. Anything else is a 400 rather than an ignored filter.

parameters.name: product_id
parameters.description: Only media the given product displays.

parameters.name: min_bytes
parameters.description: Lower bound on file size. Media recorded by URL reports zero bytes, so any lower bound excludes it.

parameters.name: max_bytes
parameters.description: Upper bound on file size. Omit for no upper bound — which is what makes "over 5 MB" expressible without a sentinel value.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description: Filter by kind.

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description: Order the page by one of these fields; omit for the listing's own order. Anything else is a 400 naming the ones that exist. Text keys are folded by PostgreSQL, and every ordering breaks ties on a key unique in the result set, so two pages of one listing never repeat or skip a row. Media recorded by URL has an empty filename and sorts last under `filename` in both directions.

200.description: A page of the library, newest first unless `sort` says otherwise.

post.description: A multipart form with a `file` field, and optionally `alt`. Accepts images, video and 3D models (glb, gltf, usdz); anything else is refused, because an upload is served back from this origin and a document or script there would be a stored-XSS vector. The uploaded filename is never used as a path — it is kept for display only. Returns 501 when the store has nowhere to put files (neither Config.MediaDir nor Config.MediaStore is set); the library still records media by URL in that case.

501.description: This store has nowhere to put uploads.

post.description: Adds a library entry for a file this store does not hold. No storage key is recorded, so deleting it only ever removes the row — nothing is ever deleted from someone else's server.

patch.description: Alt text is the only field of a stored file worth editing; everything else describes bytes that did not change.

delete.description: Refused with 409 while any product still displays it — deleting a file six products show should be a decision, not a side effect. The file itself is removed only when this store holds it.

get.summary: A product's media, in display order
get.description: Read this before writing: PUT replaces the whole ordered list, so a client that attaches one file without knowing the current one silently discards the rest.

put.summary: Set a product's media, in order
put.description: The body is the whole list, in order — a reorder and an add are the same request. Media already on the product keeps its position row, and with it any variant that nominated it; removing a file from the list also removes any variant's nomination of it.

get.summary: Whether this installation has an operator yet
get.description: Public, because it has to answer before anyone can hold a credential. The panel calls it first so a fresh database offers to create the first superuser instead of presenting a login form nobody could satisfy.

token_auth.description: A static admin token would also be accepted.

password_reset.description: An email notifier is installed, so a reset link can actually be sent. False when the only backend is the built-in logger.

post.description: Public only while no superuser exists; afterwards it is 409 for everyone. This is the one-time window that lets a fresh install become usable without shell access.

post.summary: Sign in with an email and a password
post.description: Returns a session token to send as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Wrong password and unknown operator give the identical 400, so the endpoint cannot be used to discover who has an account. Repeated failures from one address are throttled.

identity.description: The operator's email. Named `identity` for PocketBase compatibility; `email` is accepted as a synonym.

post.summary: Ask for a password reset link
post.description: Public, because a reset cannot require the credential it replaces. The answer is 202 whatever address goes in — identical in body and in status for an address that belongs to an operator and one that does not — so the route cannot be used to discover who has an account. `delivery` is `none` when the store has no email backend beyond the built-in logger; nothing will arrive, and no token is written at all. Repeated requests are throttled, on a budget separate from the login one.

identity.description: The operator's email. Named `identity` for PocketBase compatibility; `email` is accepted as a synonym.

202.description: Taken in. Whether an email is on its way is deliberately not said.

get.summary: Whether a reset link is still alive
get.description: Public: holding the token is the credential. It returns only when the link expires, so the reset screen can show a dead link before anybody types a password twice. It deliberately does not name the account — an endpoint that turned a token into an address would be the one place in this flow that confirms an operator exists.

400.description: Unknown, expired or already spent — one answer for all three.

429.description: Too many attempts from this address.

post.summary: Spend a reset link and sign in
post.description: Public. The token travels in the body rather than the path, so the one request that spends it is not repeated in an access log. It is claimed and spent in a single transaction, so two people opening one link cannot both win; every session that operator held ends with it, as does every other outstanding link of theirs, and the session in the response is new. The password is validated before the token is touched, so a typo does not burn the link.

token.description: The token from the emailed link.

400.description: An invalid or expired token, or a password that is too short.

429.description: Too many attempts from this address.

post.summary: Mail an operator a reset link
post.description: Requires `team.write`, the right that can already set that operator's password outright — so this grants nothing new, and replaces the practice of choosing somebody's password for them.

post.summary: Exchange a session for a fresh one
post.description: The panel calls this on boot to turn a stored token back into an identity, and to learn that a token has expired without waiting for a real request to fail. The old token is revoked. A static admin token is not a session and gets a 400.

patch.summary: Change an operator's email or password
patch.description: Send either field, or both. Changing the password signs that operator out everywhere, because a password change is how someone responds to a compromise.

delete.description: The last superuser cannot be removed: an admin panel nobody can sign in to is not a state an operator can click their way out of.

put.summary: Change what an operator may do
put.description: Separate from PATCH on the superuser because it is a different act: changing somebody's email is administration, changing their role is granting or taking away access. The roles are owner, manager and staff, and what each carries is fixed — see the rights list on the operator record. A store keeps at least one owner: `team.write` is the only right that can hand out roles, and demoting the last owner would leave a team where nobody carries it — so the survivors could not promote anybody, including themselves, and the way back in would be a database client. It is refused.

200.description: The operator, with their new role and the rights it carries.

parameters.name: vendor
parameters.description: Exact match.

parameters.name: product_type
parameters.description: Exact match.

parameters.name: tag
parameters.description: Products carrying exactly this tag. Exact rather than case-folded so the match is answered by the index; tags are de-duplicated case-insensitively on write, so one spelling of a tag is the only spelling stored.

parameters.name: category_id
parameters.description: Restrict to a category and everything nested under it. An unparseable value is an error rather than a silently ignored filter, because a filter that quietly matches everything is how a typo turns into "why is this showing the whole catalogue".

parameters.name: collection_id
parameters.description: Restrict to one collection's members, and order them the way that collection was curated rather than newest-first. An unparseable value is an error rather than a silently ignored filter. A collection nobody has is an empty page, not a 404. Sending `sort` together with it is a validation error rather than a silent override: a collection's order is the curation (D40).

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description: Order the page by one of these fields; omit for the listing's own order. Anything else is a 400 naming the ones that exist. Text keys are folded by PostgreSQL, and every ordering breaks ties on a key unique in the result set, so two pages of one listing never repeat or skip a row. `price` is the cheapest variant and `available` the summed availability of tracked variants; a product with no tracked variants sorts last under either, in both directions. `status` orders alphabetically (active, archived, draft), which is not the lifecycle order. Sending `sort` together with `collection_id` is a 400: a collection is shown in the order it was curated.

parameters.name: attr
parameters.description: Filter by a category attribute's recorded value, as `handle:value` — for example `attr=bag-case-material:Canvas`. Repeat the parameter to add more. Several values of the SAME handle widen the result (canvas OR leather, because a shopper who ticks both wants either); different handles narrow it (canvas AND black, because they describe one item). Only the first colon separates, so `color:Black:ish` is the value "Black:ish". Matching is exact, not a substring. An entry with no colon, no handle or no value is ignored rather than refused, so a truncated URL narrows to everything or to nothing instead of taking the listing away. The values are the ones stored under `metadata.category` by the category's own field list.

post.description: Options and variants may be created in the same call. For a product with no options, send `sku` and `price_minor` instead of `variants` and the single default variant is created for you.

get.summary: Get a product in any status

patch.description: Every field is optional; an omitted field is left alone, which is what distinguishes "not mentioned" from "set to empty".

tags.description: Replaces the whole set. Tags have no identity of their own, so "add one" is not something the engine can tell apart from a client that sent a stale list.

delete.description: Order lines survive: they hold their own snapshot and their product reference is simply nulled.

put.description:
Sets the whole matrix and reconciles the variants with it in one transaction — which is what an editor needs, since renaming an axis or dropping a value is a single intent that would leave the product incoherent if split across calls.

Send an option's `id` to keep it: matched by name alone, renaming "Size" to "Größe" is indistinguishable from deleting one axis and adding another, and every variant would lose its size. Omit `id` for a new axis. A value carries an id for the same reason — send `{"id": 7, "value": "Crimson"}` to rename the value that row 7 holds, and a bare `"Crimson"` to add a new one.

A variant whose combination survives is left completely alone — price, SKU and stock included. A variant whose combination no longer exists is deleted; its order lines keep their own snapshot, so history stays readable. New combinations are created only when `generate_variants` is set.

The same value may not appear on two axes: variant options are resolved by value, so "Small" as both a Size and a Cup could not be told apart, and the request is refused rather than silently mis-resolved.

id.description: The existing axis this replaces. Omit for a new one.

values.description: The axis's values, in display order. A bare string is a value with no identity — what every client sent before value ids existed, and still the right shape for a matrix being created. Send `{id, value}` to keep a value: matched by text alone, renaming "Red" to "Crimson" is a delete plus an add, and every Red variant's price, SKU, image and stock goes with it.

id.description: The existing value this replaces. Omit for a new one; an id this axis does not have is refused rather than treated as new.

generate_variants.description: Create a variant for every combination that has none. Off by default: adding an axis should not quietly mint sellable SKUs at a guessed price.

price_minor.description: Price for generated variants. Omitted copies the product's existing default.

200.description: The reconciled product, and what changed.

post.description: `options` names the value chosen on each of the product's axes, in any order. Two variants may not select the same combination — that is enforced by a unique index, not by hope.

put.description: Replace, not merge: the caller holds the whole list. An "add" endpoint quietly re-creates a membership the operator removed in another tab, with no way for them to see that it happened. The order sent is the order stored, an unknown id rejects the whole request, and an empty list clears membership. The `position` it writes is where each collection sits in THIS product's list, not where this product sits in each collection — that is `member_position`, which only PUT /api/admin/collections/{id}/products writes (D40).

get.description: Every collection, including the empty ones the public listing hides.

200.description: A page of collections, ordered by position then id.

patch.description: Every field is optional; an omitted field is left alone.

delete.description: The products in it survive. A collection groups products, it does not own them, so deleting "Summer sale" must not delete the summer stock — only the membership rows go.

get.description: In the order the collection was curated, drafts included — staging them is what an operator is doing here. 404 rather than an empty page for a collection that does not exist, which is what a curation screen needs to know before it offers to reorder anything. It takes the same filter vocabulary as the product listing, except `collection_id`: the path already names the collection, so sending one is a 400 rather than a filter nobody would notice being dropped.

parameters.name: vendor
parameters.description: Exact match.

parameters.name: product_type
parameters.description: Exact match.

parameters.name: tag
parameters.description: Products carrying exactly this tag. Exact rather than case-folded so the match is answered by the index; tags are de-duplicated case-insensitively on write, so one spelling of a tag is the only spelling stored.

parameters.name: category_id
parameters.description: Restrict to a category and everything nested under it. An unparseable value is an error rather than a silently ignored filter, because a filter that quietly matches everything is how a typo turns into "why is this showing the whole catalogue".

put.description: Replace, not merge, for the reason the product-side route gives: the caller holds the whole list — INCLUDING the memberships it never fetched, which are deleted. A screen must hold the entire membership before it saves. The order sent is the order stored, and it is the only way a collection's own order is ever chosen — it writes `member_position`, never the `position` that orders a collection inside one product's own list (D40). `product_ids` is required: omitting it is a 400, and an explicit empty array is how a collection is emptied without being deleted. An unknown product id rejects the whole request. The answer is 204: the useful response would be the whole membership, and a page of it is a list a client could re-save from and lose the tail — read it back with the GET above.

204.description: The membership is what was sent.

patch.description: Stock is deliberately not patchable here. Inventory moves through its own endpoint so that every change is a transactional adjustment rather than a blind overwrite of a number another request may have just changed.

compare_at_price_minor.description: The price a storefront strikes through. Send null to take the item off sale; omit the field to leave it alone. Negative is a 400.

continue_selling.description: Take the order when the count has run out, instead of refusing it.

origin_country.description: Where the item was made, ISO 3166-1 alpha-2.

cost_minor.description: Send null to clear a recorded cost.

size.description: Only the sides named are written, so changing the height does not erase a length somebody measured earlier.

dimension_unit.description: The unit the sides in `size` are given in, and the unit they are read back in. Sending this alone re-reads the sides already stored in the new unit: the millimetres are the fact, and switching units changes how the box is read, not how big it is. A patch that wants exact millimetres names "mm" here — there is one way to give a side rather than two that can disagree.

delete.description: A product must keep at least one variant: a product with nothing sellable is not a product.

post.description:
Send `adjust` to move the count by a delta (receiving stock), or `set` to replace it (a stock take). Neither may leave on-hand below the quantity already reserved at that location for orders in flight.

`location_id` says which shelf; omit it for the default one, which is what a single-location store always means.

Refused with 409 when the receiving location is closed: stock moves out of a closed location, never into it. Every decrease is still allowed, including at a closed one, because emptying a closed shelf is the only way it is ever cleared.

reason.description: Optional. Why the stock moved, recorded verbatim in the stock ledger — a delivery, a damage write-off, a recount. The panel asks for one on a count and on a write-off; the engine accepts a blank from any client.

get.summary: Variants at or below a stock threshold

parameters.name: location_id
parameters.description: Without it the threshold is against the store's total, which is what a single-location store means: a variant with one unit in each of five shops is not low by that reading, even though every shelf looks it. With it, the threshold is against that location alone and each row carries `at_location`. Only variants the location already has a stock row for are considered.

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description: Order the page by one of these fields; omit for the report's own order, which is emptiest first. Anything else is a 400 naming the ones that exist. Text keys are folded by PostgreSQL, and every ordering breaks ties on the variant id, so two pages of one report never repeat or skip a row. The three stock keys follow `location_id`: without it they are the store-wide sums shown on the row, and with it they are that one location's own numbers — the same figures `at_location` carries, so the column being sorted is always the column being read.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: The operator's search box. Matches an order number from the start, or an email or a name containing it, case-insensitively. `email` is the exact-match filter and still works beside it; the two are ANDed, never ORed.

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description: Order the page by one of these fields; omit for the listing's own order. Anything else is a 400 naming the ones that exist. Text keys are folded by PostgreSQL, and every ordering breaks ties on a key unique in the result set, so two pages of one listing never repeat or skip a row. `number` orders by the id the number is built from, which stays true past six digits where a text sort does not; `total` orders by `total_minor`. Orders with no customer name sort last in both directions.

post.summary: Place an order on a customer's behalf
post.description: The phone order, the trade counter, the replacement parcel. It builds a cart and checks it out rather than inserting an order, so the result is indistinguishable from one a shopper placed: stock is reserved under the same lock, prices are snapshotted the same way, and the same order.created event reaches every notifier. The order carries an access token, so the customer can look it up without an account. Distinct from POST /api/admin/import/orders, which records orders that already happened elsewhere and deliberately moves no stock.

payment_method.description: Code of a registered payment method.

email.description: Required: the order is looked up by it, and notifications go to it.

metadata.description: A `notes` key is refused with a 400: it is reserved for the shop's own note on the order, which is set through PATCH /api/admin/orders/{id}.

discount_code.description: Optional. A promotion code the operator is honouring — the one the customer quoted on the telephone. It is judged by the checkout under its own lock, exactly as a shopper's is, so an expired, exhausted or ineligible code refuses the whole request with 422 and no order is created and no stock is reserved.

201.description: The order and what must happen to pay for it. `data.order.access_token` is returned here and in no other admin *read*: it is the guest's only credential for their own order, so no listing and no GET carries it. A customer who has lost their link is helped with POST /api/admin/orders/{id}/access-token, which reads the same token back out under `orders.write` and writes an audit row saying who asked.

get.description: Baskets that have not become orders yet: what is in them, what they are worth, and the address to reach the shopper on. Read-only and tokenless - a cart's token is a live credential, so it is never returned here and a cart is addressed by its numeric row id. `state` is derived from the status column AND `expires_at`, so a cart the five-minute sweeper has not reached yet still reports as abandoned.

parameters.name: state
parameters.description: Derived from status and expires_at, not the status column alone.

parameters.name: has_lines
parameters.description: Counts lines rather than value, so a basket of free samples is never silently dropped.

parameters.name: min_value_minor
parameters.description: Minimum basket value, in the currency's minor units - quantity x the snapshotted unit price.

200.description: A page of carts, newest first.

get.description: One basket and what is in it, addressed by the numeric id the listing reports. Each line carries both coordinates - the price as snapshotted and the price now - so an operator can see whether the basket is still worth chasing. Still no token.

get.summary: The orders, grouped by who placed them
get.description: There is no customer resource behind this. Guest checkout is a permanent guarantee (D22), so a shopper never has an account and an order carries its own snapshot of who bought it — which means a customer can only be every order sharing an email. Name, phone and address come from that person's most recent order. Orders counts everything they placed that was not cancelled; spent totals only what was actually paid, so an order awaiting cash on delivery is a real order and not yet money. Correcting a customer means correcting an order, which is why there is no GET by id, PATCH or DELETE here.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Matches an email or a name, case-insensitively.

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description: Order the page by one of these fields; omit for the listing's own order. Anything else is a 400 naming the ones that exist. Text keys are folded by PostgreSQL, and every ordering breaks ties on a key unique in the result set, so two pages of one listing never repeat or skip a row. Every key is the grouping key or an aggregate over it, so the ordering is on the same number the row shows. There is no `id` key: the listing has no id.

orders.description: Orders placed that were not cancelled.

patch.summary: Correct an order's contact details and payment record
patch.description:
An email with a typo in it means the customer never hears from the shop again; an address with the wrong house number means the parcel goes to the wrong door; a payment reference is what somebody reconciles against a bank statement. None of them is a state change, and each is a field a person typed once.

Correcting an address does not move a parcel that has already gone out.

get.description:
Every state change writes its event and its audit record in the same transaction that caused it, so this is the order's history rather than a log kept beside it: what happened, in what order, who did it, and whether the notification it triggered actually went out. An act that announced something renders once, carrying both halves.

`published_at` is set only once every subscribed handler accepted the event; `attempts` above one and `dead` say a consumer is failing, and `last_error` says why — that field is returned only to an operator carrying `store.operate`, and is absent otherwise. Entries with no actor are ones the trail did not record: everything that happened before it existed, and the engine's own sweeps before they were attributed.

post.summary: Read an order's guest access token back out
post.description:
The customer rang: they have lost the "view your order" link. The access token is their only credential — guest checkout is permanent (D22), so there is no account to sign into — and it is returned at checkout and by nothing else, which left a support desk with no answer at all.

It reveals the existing token rather than issuing a new one. Rotating would answer the same question while silently breaking the link in the confirmation mail the customer already has, so an operator helping with a mislaid link would be destroying the mislaid copy.

POST, not GET, and `orders.write`, not `orders.read`: handing out a bearer credential is an act, and it is recorded as one. Every call writes an `order.token_reveal` row naming the operator, in the same transaction as the read — the token itself is deliberately not in that row, because an append-only table nothing can delete from is the last place a live credential should be copied into. No body.

200.description: The order's number and its access token.

access_token.description: Pass it to GET /api/orders/{number}?token=… — that is the whole of the customer's flow.

post.description: Returns the inventory. Which movement is correct depends on how far the order got: a pending order only ever reserved stock, while a confirmed one has already taken it off the shelf. An order that has shipped cannot be cancelled — that is a return.

How cash on delivery is settled, and the same call a gateway module makes from its webhook. It also confirms a pending order — without that, a paid order would wait forever for a step nobody performs. Idempotent: a replayed webhook does not commit stock twice.

Goes back through the provider that took the money. A method that cannot refund — cash on delivery, for one — reports that plainly rather than pretending. Omit the amount to send back everything that has not been refunded yet. An order may be refunded in parts; payment_status stays paid until they add up to the total, and refunded carries the running figure. This moves money only: goods coming back are recorded as a return, which is what puts them on the shelf.

amount_minor.description: Omitted, zero or negative means everything still refundable, counting a refund already in flight.

reason.description: Why the money went back. Recorded on the refund and carried on the event, so whatever tells the customer can say it.

post.description: Records goods coming back off a shipped, partly shipped or delivered order, and puts back on the shelf the lines marked to restock. It moves no money: refunding is POST /api/admin/orders/{id}/refund, a separate operation with its own right and its own record, and the two are recorded separately on purpose. Quantities are per line and cumulative across returns — more than is still owed is refused — and on a partly shipped order only what has actually gone out can come back. The order's status and payment_status are untouched, because the delivery still happened.

reason.description: Why it came back. Customer-visible: it rides the order.returned event out to the notifiers, as a cancellation reason does.

lines.description: What came back. At least one, each naming a line of this order at most once.

line_id.description: A line of this order, as returned in line_items[].id.

quantity.description: How many units came back. No more than what is still returnable: what went out, less what has already come back on returns that still stand.

restock.description: Whether these units go back on sale. Absent means false, so nothing moves unless somebody says it should — a damaged item is still returned, it simply moves no stock.

location_id.description: Which shelf they go back on. Absent or 0 means the one the line was picked from. A named location must be active.

201.description: The order as it now stands, and the return that was recorded.

delete.summary: Withdraw a return recorded in error
delete.description: Takes back a return that should not have been recorded. The row survives with status withdrawn — how much is still returnable is counted from these rows, and a return whose row is gone is a stock movement nobody can account for — and the units it put back come off the shelf again. Withdrawing an already-withdrawn return is a silent no-op. It is refused when those units have since gone out again, because taking them off would push the count below what other orders have reserved.

post.summary: Settle a refund that was never heard back about
post.description: The recovery path for a process that died between the gateway accepting a refund and the store recording it. The engine cannot know whether the money left; a person looking at the gateway can, and this is how they say so — rather than by writing SQL against the ledger. A refund younger than fifteen minutes may still be in flight and is refused.

provider_reference.description: The gateway's id for the refund, when it did go out.

note.description: What the gateway said, when it did not.

put.summary: Change what is on an order
put.description: Replaces the order's lines with the set given. A line the order already has is named by its id; one being added names a variant instead, and is priced as that variant is priced today. A line the request leaves out is removed, and an order may not be left with none — cancel it instead. Stock moves with the change: an order that has only reserved its stock has its reservation adjusted, one that has already taken the units off the shelf gives them back or takes more. The money is not settled here — the response reports the totals either side of the edit and the balance between them, and collecting or refunding it is a payment operation with its own record. An order that has shipped, been cancelled or been refunded cannot be edited.

id.description: A line the order already has. Omit for a new one.

variant_id.description: The variant to add. Required when id is absent.

quantity.description: Zero removes a line the order already has.

200.description: The order, and what the edit changed.

post.description: Books a shipment against some or all of an order, and lets the order's status follow what has gone out: `shipped` when nothing is left, `partial` while units are still owed. Omitting `lines` ships everything the order still owes, so the same request sent twice ships the whole order and then the remainder. With the built-in `manual` provider an operator packs the box and types the tracking number; a carrier module reads `meta` for its own options, such as courier choice or pickup slot.

carrier.description: Who is carrying it, as a carrier code. Worked out from the tracking number when left out.

lines.description: What goes in this parcel. Omit it to ship everything the order still owes, which on a first shipment is the whole order.

order_line_id.description: A line the order already has, as returned in line_items[].id.

get.description: One row per variant. Cells beginning with =, +, - or @ are prefixed with an apostrophe, because a spreadsheet executes those on open; import strips exactly one back, so the round trip stays lossless. It takes the same filters as the admin product listing — q, status, vendor, product_type, tag, category_id and collection_id — so a reconciliation can export exactly the rows a screen is showing. There is no paging: an export streams every row that matched. Row order stays p.id, v.position, v.id whatever the filters are, because the importer requires a product's variant rows to be contiguous.

parameters.name: vendor
parameters.description: Exact match.

parameters.name: product_type
parameters.description: Exact match.

parameters.name: tag
parameters.description: Products carrying exactly this tag. Exact rather than case-folded so the match is answered by the index; tags are de-duplicated case-insensitively on write, so one spelling of a tag is the only spelling stored.

parameters.name: category_id
parameters.description: Restrict to a category and everything nested under it. An unparseable value is an error rather than a silently ignored filter, because a filter that quietly matches everything is how a typo turns into "why is this showing the whole catalogue".

parameters.name: collection_id
parameters.description: Restrict to one collection's members, and order them the way that collection was curated rather than newest-first. An unparseable value is an error rather than a silently ignored filter. A collection nobody has is an empty page, not a 404. If a sort parameter is ever added to this listing, sending it together with collection_id must be a validation error rather than a silent override: a collection's order is the curation (D40).

post.description:
Upserts by SKU. Rows for one product must be contiguous — which is what export produces — so a large file streams instead of being held in memory. A bad row is reported with its line number and never aborts the file.

A `stock_on_hand:<code>` cell that raises the count at a closed location fails that row, naming the code: stock moves out of a closed location, never into it. A cell at or below the current count is accepted, so an unedited export of a closed location's zeros still imports.

get.description: One row per order line, with the order's columns repeated — the shape an accountant's pivot table wants.

One row per person — the mailing list a shop actually asks this screen for. A customer is a reading of the orders and not a table (see GET /api/admin/customers), so the columns are the same aggregates the listing shows: name, phone and address from that person's most recent order, orders not cancelled, and lifetime spend as `spent_minor` plus `currency` rather than a formatted amount. `q` and `sort` are the listing's own, so a file taken off a filtered screen is the rows on that screen. There is no matching import: there is no customer record to write back into.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Matches an email or a name, case-insensitively — the same predicate the listing uses.

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description: Order the file by one of these fields; omit for the listing's own order, most recent buyer first. Anything else is a 400 — issued before a byte of CSV is written, which is the only moment it still can be.

post.description: For migrating from another platform. It does not touch inventory — those stock movements happened on the old system — and it fires no events unless `fire_events` is set, because importing five thousand orders must not send five thousand confirmation emails. An order whose number already exists is skipped, so re-importing an export is a no-op.

An empty body imports the embedded Shopify taxonomy — ~14,000 categories, idempotent on (parent, title), so running it twice adds only what is missing. A body is the operator's own file in the published `gid : A > B > C` format. The embedded set also imports the field definitions in the same call, because they match on the taxonomy id this import writes and a tree from anywhere else has nothing to match. One transaction: half a taxonomy is worse than none. It can take minutes; the request extends its own read and write deadlines past the server's, and a client that disconnects rolls the transaction back.

An empty body imports the embedded dictionary; a body is the operator's own file in the two-section `handle = Label : v | v` then `gid : handle, handle` format. It attaches field lists to categories already carrying a taxonomy id, so it follows the tree rather than preceding it — against a tree from somewhere else every line is unmatched. The dictionary rows themselves are upserted, so a store's own entries survive. Same extended deadlines as the tree import.

get.description: Nested by default, because a storefront menu is nested. `?flat=1` returns the same rows depth-first, which is what an indented picker wants: every row carries `depth` and `child_count`, so a client can indent and expand without rebuilding the tree.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Search titles and paths, case-insensitively.

parameters.name: parent
parameters.description: `root`, or a category id: return that node's direct children only.

parameters.name: flat
parameters.description: Return a depth-first flat list instead of nested children.

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description: Order the page by one of these fields; omit for the listing's own order. Anything else is a 400 naming the ones that exist. Text keys are folded by PostgreSQL, and every ordering breaks ties on a key unique in the result set, so two pages of one listing never repeat or skip a row. Honoured only on the `?q=` search branch; sent with `?parent=`, `?flat=1` or a whole-tree listing it is a 400, because a tree's order is the position an operator gave it. The sort is applied before the limit, so `sort=title` returns the alphabetically first matches rather than the shallowest ones alphabetised. `full_name` orders by the rendered path, which is what the row shows.

200.description: The tree, or the flattened list.

get.summary: A category and the products filed under it
get.description: Descendants are included, because that is what picking a category means: someone who asks for Apparel wants the shirts too, and a filter that returned only products filed at the exact node would show an empty page for every branch. The meta describes the products, since they are the pageable part.

200.description: The category flattened into the response, with a page of its products.

get.summary: List, search or browse the tree
get.description: Three shapes from one route. `?q=` searches the whole tree and answers with a bounded flat set of paths, which is the normal way to work once a full taxonomy is imported. `?parent=root` or `?parent={id}` returns one level, the shape a browsable picker asks for, bounded by construction. Neither, and the whole tree comes back, but only while it is small enough to send honestly: past that the response is a bounded slice whose `meta.total` reports the real size, so a client that compares the two can see it holds only a part and switch to searching.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Search titles and paths, case-insensitively.

parameters.name: parent
parameters.description: `root`, or a category id: return that node's direct children only.

parameters.name: flat
parameters.description: Depth-first flat list instead of nested children.

Honoured only on the `?q=` search branch; sent with `?parent=`, `?flat=1` or a whole-tree listing it is a 400, because a tree's order is the position an operator gave it. The sort is applied before the limit, so `sort=title` returns the alphabetically first matches rather than the shallowest ones alphabetised. `full_name` orders by the rendered path, which is what the row shows.

200.description: Categories. `meta.total` is the real size of the tree, which can exceed what was sent; on a search it stays the true number of matches even when the requested window is past the end of them.

delete.description: Refused while anything still points at it, whether a subcategory or a product filed under it. Deleting a branch is not a way to lose what was in it, so the references have to be moved first.

get.summary: The branch a category sits on, root first
get.description: The chain from the root down to this category, the category itself last. A client that holds one category and needs what the whole branch says about it cannot get there from the listing — a store carrying a full taxonomy has thousands of categories and the listing sends a page — so the chain is asked for by id. Each node carries its metadata, which is where a category declares the fields it asks of a product. An unknown id comes back as an empty list rather than a 404: it is a category deleted while somebody had the product open.
The store-wide field dictionary: a handle, what the field is called, and the values it offers wherever a category asks for it. Ordered by handle, because a dictionary's order is its spelling.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Matches a handle or a label, case-folded.

post.summary: Add a field to the dictionary
post.description: The handle is supplied rather than derived from the label: it is the key a category's metadata names, so deriving it would make renaming a label orphan every category using the field. It is folded to lower case and may carry neither whitespace nor a slash. Choices keep the order sent — "XS, S, M, L, XL" is the publisher's order and the only useful one — with blanks and exact repeats dropped.

parameters.name: handle
parameters.description: The key a category's metadata names, e.g. `animal-type`. Folded to lower case, because the match against a category's metadata is literal and the column is the primary key.

patch.description: Label and choices only. The handle is not patchable and sending it is a 400 rather than a silent no-op: it is the key every category's metadata holds, and renaming it here would detach them all without saying so. Moving a field to a new handle is a create, an edit of the categories that name it, and a delete. A sent `choices` array replaces the whole list.

parameters.name: handle
parameters.description: The key a category's metadata names, e.g. `animal-type`. Folded to lower case, because the match against a category's metadata is literal and the column is the primary key.

delete.description: Never refused. A category that still names the handle keeps the field and simply offers no fixed choices, which is a free-text field rather than a broken one.

parameters.name: handle
parameters.description: The key a category's metadata names, e.g. `animal-type`. Folded to lower case, because the match against a category's metadata is literal and the column is the primary key.

put.summary: Set or clear a variant's pictures
put.description: Replaces the list of the product's pictures this variant shows, in the order given. Every id in `media_ids` must already be on the variant's product — a variant nominates some of the product's pictures rather than owning files, which is what lets every size of a colour show the same photographs stored once, and attaching from here would put a picture at a position in the product's ordered list that nobody chose. Send `[]` to clear. `media_id` is the shape from before there was a list — one picture, or `null` to clear — and still works. One of the two is required: an omitted field is a 400 rather than a guess, because guessing is how pictures get removed by a request that never mentioned them.

schema.description: One of the two fields is required.

media_ids.description: The pictures, in display order; `[]` clears. Each must already be on the variant's product.

media_id.description: One picture, or null to clear — the shape from before the list. Ignored when `media_ids` is present.

200.description: The variant, with the pictures the store now holds.

post.summary: Take back a payment status recorded in error
post.description:
A correction, not a refund: it says the money never arrived and somebody marked the wrong order, so it leaves no refund behind. It moves the payment status and nothing else — a confirmed order awaiting payment is not a broken state, it is what every cash-on-delivery order already is, and un-confirming would put stock back on the shelf while the order is still live. An operator who wants the stock back cancels the order instead.

Refused on a refunded order, where money really did move, and on a cancelled one.

It clears a recorded failure as well: an order whose payment is `failed` goes back to `pending` and loses its payment reference, silently — the failure was never announced, so its reversal announces nothing. On an already-pending order it does nothing.

post.summary: Record a payment attempt that did not succeed
post.description:
The order stays where it is — it is not cancelled and its stock is not released — so the shopper can try again. Its reservation stays in the sweeper's reach, so an attempt nobody retries eventually cancels the order and returns the stock on its own.

Two deliberate no-ops answer 200 and change nothing: an order whose payment is already failed, and an order that has been cancelled. The cancelled case is checked first, so a late gateway callback for an order the sweeper already cancelled is recorded as nothing rather than refused — a 409 there is a webhook retried forever.

Refused with 409 on an order that is already paid, and on one that was refunded, where money really did move.

`POST /api/admin/orders/{id}/mark-unpaid` takes a recorded failure back.

reason.description: Optional. Written to the store's log and nowhere else: it is not stored on the order and never returned. The panel sends a fixed string rather than prompting for prose it would discard.

post.summary: Take back a delivery recorded in error
post.description: The order returns to shipped, and so do the fulfillments that were marked delivered with it. Nothing moved when the delivery was recorded — no stock, no money — so nothing moves back. Refused from any status but delivered.

patch.description: Typing a tracking number is the one step of shipping a parcel nobody else checks, so it is the one that gets mistyped. This changes what was recorded about the shipment and nothing about the order: the parcel left either way, and correcting the number is not un-shipping it.

delete.summary: Remove a shipment recorded in error
delete.description:
The order follows it. "Shipped" was true because that record existed, so removing the last one that says so puts the order back to confirmed — leaving it shipped with nothing shipping it would be a state no operation could explain and no operator could correct.

Refused on a delivered order: a parcel somebody received is not a record to erase, and undoing the delivery first is the operation that says so.

Returns the order, whose status may have moved with the shipment.

get.summary: Carriers, or the ones a tracking number could belong to
get.description:
Without `tracking`, every carrier the engine can name. With it, the ones whose numbering the number fits, best first.

That is a list rather than a verdict on purpose. A tracking number is not self-describing: several carriers issue bare ten- to fourteen-digit numbers, so a twelve-digit number is genuinely ambiguous. Where a number carries something distinctive — UPS's `1Z`, the S10 standard's country suffix, DHL's `JJD` — the list has one entry and a client can fill the field in. Where it does not, the operator picks. Guessing would hand the customer a tracking link that goes nowhere, which reads as the shop having lost their parcel.

parameters.name: tracking
parameters.description: Return only the carriers this number could belong to.

put.summary: Put a discount code on a cart
put.description: Answers with what the code is worth for this basket. That amount is a preview, not a promise: nothing is consumed here, and checkout decides again under its own lock. A code that is valid now and exhausted in ten minutes is refused then, which is the only honest place to refuse it. A cart that has already been checked out refuses this: there is nothing left to discount, and the row would be one nothing reads. A scoped code is refused when this basket holds none of the products, collections or categories it names — a valid code can be refused for this basket alone, and the message says so.

email.description: Optional. `once_per_email` cannot be previewed without it.

delete.summary: Take the discount code off a cart
delete.description: Clearing the code is the same write as setting one, with an empty code. A cart that has already been checked out refuses this for the same reason PUT does.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Match the title or the code.

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description: Order the page by one of these fields; omit for the listing's own order. Anything else is a 400 naming the ones that exist. Text keys are folded by PostgreSQL, and every ordering breaks ties on a key unique in the result set, so two pages of one listing never repeat or skip a row. Automatic discounts have no code and sort last in both directions. There is no key for the state chip or for what the rule takes off: the first is derived from five columns at once, and the second mixes basis points with minor units.

200.description: Discounts, newest first unless `sort` says otherwise.
The discount, plus what it has actually cost.

patch.description: `used_count` cannot be written: it is a fact about what happened, and letting an operator type over it would silently reopen a promotion that has been fully used. `target_ids` absent leaves the stored set alone; a list replaces it whole, because the caller holds the whole list; `[]` clears it, which is refused while the resulting scope is still products, collections or categories. Setting `scope` to `order` clears the targets in the same transaction without needing `target_ids`. Moving the scope to or between the other three requires `target_ids` in the same body — the targets it would otherwise inherit are of the wrong kind. A patch that changes only `target_ids` is a real edit and bumps `updated_at`. (This operation still references DiscountInput rather than a DiscountPatch schema, so the field documents both verbs by accident rather than by design.)

delete.description: Orders that used it keep their snapshot and read correctly.

get.description:
What a promotion has actually been spent on, newest first. The rows are the snapshots taken at checkout, so a rule that has since been renamed still reads as what it was.

Cancelled orders are listed here, marked by their status, and excluded from the detail's `redeemed_total` — so `meta.total` counts more orders than `redeemed_orders` whenever any were cancelled.

Needs both `discounts.read` and `orders.read`: the row carries an order number, an email address and a total.

A deleted rule's redemptions are unreachable here, because `order_discounts.discount_id` is `ON DELETE SET NULL` and the snapshots stay with their orders.

post.summary: Try a discount against a basket
post.description:
A dry run, so a new promotion's first test is not a real customer. Nothing is locked, nothing is written and no usage is claimed, so a preview can never exhaust a code.

A rule that would not apply comes back as `applies: false` with the reason, not as an error — the question was whether it works, and "no, it expired on Friday" is a successful answer to it. Reasons include an expired or unstarted window, an inactive rule, a usage limit reached, a basket below the minimum, a code already used by that email address, a scope holding nothing in this basket, and a codeless automatic rule, which nothing evaluates at checkout yet.

Send `subtotal_minor` for an order-wide rule, or `lines` for a scoped one — a scoped rule comes off the lines its targets reach, which a bare total cannot say. Sending both is a 400.

The request being wrong is still an error: an unknown id is 404 and a negative amount is 400.

subtotal_minor.description: The basket to try it against, in minor units. Use this or `lines`, not both.

email.description: Optional. `once_per_email` cannot be previewed without it.

lines.description: The basket line by line, for a scoped rule. A scoped rule previewed with a bare subtotal answers `applies: false` saying the lines are missing, rather than reporting an amount it cannot know.

200.description: What the rule would do, or why it would not.

get.summary: List tax rates, most specific first
get.description: The order they come back in is the order they are applied in, so a reader can see which rule wins without reproducing the resolution.

post.description: One rule per country, state and category. A second rule covering the same three is refused: that is a mistake to catch at entry, not a preference to resolve at checkout.

patch.description: Changing a rate affects what is charged from now on and nothing already sold. What each order was charged is stored on its lines, so an invoice prints the same figures next year as it does today.

delete.description: Orders keep what they were charged.

get.description: In the order stock is drawn from them: lowest priority first.

post.description: A new location holds nothing and is not made default — that would silently redirect every future reservation as a side effect of adding a shelf. Move stock into it with the variant transfer endpoint.

patch.description: Deactivating one that still holds stock is refused, and the error names how many units are stranded: an inactive location would have its units counted in `stock_on_hand` while nothing could reserve them.

delete.description: Refused while it holds stock, and refused for the default one — something has to answer "where does this land". Orders already filled from here keep reading; their lines simply stop naming a place.

get.summary: Everything that moved at one location
get.description: The same ledger from the other end: everything that has moved at one location, newest first. A location that has been deleted answers 404 — its rows stay readable on the variant route, where the location_code snapshot still names where the units were.

parameters.name: variant_id
parameters.description: Narrow to one SKU.

parameters.name: order_id
parameters.description: Only what one order caused.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description: One or more movement kinds, comma-separated or repeated. An unknown kind is a 400 rather than an empty page.

post.description: The default is where stock lands when nothing names a place: new variants, CSV imports, and every client written before locations existed. Exactly one location is the default, so this moves it rather than adding one.

get.description: The inverse of `GET /api/admin/variants/{id}/stock`: what one place is holding, rather than where one variant is. Each row carries `at_location` beside the variant's store-wide figures, so "the store has 40, this shelf has none" is one row rather than two requests. Only variants this location already has a stock row for appear — one it has never carried is not a shelf it can restock.

parameters.name: nonzero
parameters.description: Defaults to true. A row is held when `on_hand` or `reserved` is non-zero, the same test that refuses a close, so this listing and that refusal always agree about what is there. `nonzero=0` adds the rows sitting at zero.

200.description: Variants held here, most units first.

get.description: The variant's own `stock_on_hand` and `stock_reserved` are the sums of these rows. This is the breakdown a picker, a stock take or a delivery estimate actually needs.

get.summary: How a variant's stock got here
get.description: The append-only stock ledger for one variant, newest first. One row per real change, carrying two signed deltas, the balances after, what kind of movement it was, which path caused it, the operator's reason and the order behind it. Ordered by id rather than by created_at: a transfer writes both of its rows in one transaction and they share the instant exactly. Behind inventory.read, because reading how a count got there is reading stock.

parameters.name: location_id
parameters.description: Narrow to one shelf.

parameters.name: order_id
parameters.description: Only what one order caused.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description: One or more movement kinds, comma-separated or repeated. An unknown kind is a 400 rather than an empty page.

post.description:
One statement out and one in, in a single transaction, so the store's total never changes even for an instant. Reserved units do not travel: they are promised to orders that will be picked from where they are, and moving them would send a picker to the wrong shelf.

Refused with 409 when `to_location_id` is closed: stock moves out of a closed location, never into it. The **source** may be closed, and always could be — that is the recovery path for a store that already has units stranded at one.

from_location_id.description: Required. There is no default shelf to take units off, and guessing would empty one the operator never named.

reason.description: Optional. Why the units moved — rebalancing, a store request. Recorded verbatim on BOTH ends of the transfer, because the row that says they left and the row that says they arrived are one act.

200.description: The variant, with its totals unchanged.

get.description: Outstanding first, then accepted ones most recent first. Accepted invitations are kept so the team screen can answer who let somebody in.

post.description:
Returns the invitation with its `token` and `accept_url` — the only response that ever carries them. Send the link; the invitee chooses their own password and nobody else ever sees it.

Re-inviting an address replaces the outstanding invitation, so the previous link stops working. An address that already belongs to an operator is refused: changing somebody's role has its own endpoint, and it cannot be used to hand out a fresh password.

delete.description: Closes an outstanding link. An accepted invitation is history and cannot be revoked — remove the operator instead.

get.summary: See what an invitation is for

get.description:
The same checks `gocommerce doctor` runs and the MCP `store_health` tool returns — the database, the migration ledger, admin access, the outbox, stock reservations, carts, the catalog, the registered providers, this contract, admin route gating, fulfillment, refunds, returns, the stock ledger and discounts.

It answers 200 even when `ok` is false, because the report is the answer rather than the error: a non-2xx would send a client down its error path at the one moment the detail matters most. `/health/ready` keeps its 503 because an orchestrator needs a status code; a person needs the detail.

A check that failed because it could not run records the underlying driver text separately from its finding, and this response never carries it — a pgx error names a host, a port and a user, and the rest of this API refuses to send those to a client. It is written to the store's log instead. `gocommerce doctor` and `doctor -json` still print it.

200.description: The report, whether or not the store is well.

post.description:
Runs the three cart phases in one pass: an expired basket holding something is marked abandoned and announced as `cart.abandoned`, an expired basket holding nothing is deleted, and an abandoned one is deleted once `Config.CartRetention` has run out. The route runs the same service method the engine's own five-minute ticker runs — there is no second state machine and no panel-only maintenance path.

Each phase is bounded, so a store carrying a backlog clears it over successive presses rather than in one statement; `capped` says a phase filled its batch and there is more to do.

The body is ignored — send `{}`.

abandoned.description: Expired baskets with lines in them, marked abandoned and announced.

purged.description: Abandoned baskets deleted because they are past Config.CartRetention.

capped.description: A phase filled its batch; press again for the rest.

post.summary: Release stock held by unpaid orders
post.description:
Cancels pending orders whose payment never settled — pending or failed — past their reservation window, returning their stock to the shelf. Each cancellation is its own transaction and emits the ordinary `order.cancelled` event with the reason "payment not completed in time". The route runs the same service method the engine's own five-minute ticker runs — there is no second state machine and no panel-only maintenance path.

One pass, never a loop, and safe to press twice: cancelling an already-cancelled order does nothing. An order the service could not cancel is logged and skipped, which lowers `cancelled` without lowering what the pass found — which is why `capped` is derived from what was found.

The body is ignored — send `{}`.

cancelled.description: Expired unsettled orders this pass actually cancelled.

capped.description: The pass examined a full batch of 200 expired orders, so there may be more. Derived from what it found, not from what it cancelled: a backlog where some cancellations failed still says "press again" rather than "queue clear".

post.summary: Force a delivery pass on the outbox
post.description:
Delivers every event that is due, synchronously, instead of waiting for the dispatcher's poll. It is the same delivery path the background dispatcher runs, and the two can run at once: `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` keeps their claims disjoint.

`delivered` counts rows claimed, not rows a handler accepted. A handler that errors leaves its row for the dispatcher's backoff, which is what at-least-once means. And a drain does not resurrect dead-lettered rows — those are excluded from the claim by design, and requeueing one is a separate act.

The pass has a 30-second budget, checked between batches and never inside one: a batch is claimed whole before any of it is dispatched, so cutting one short would burn a retry on every event it had claimed and not yet reached. `capped: true` therefore means a partial pass, not a failure. One pass at a time per process; a second request while one is running is refused rather than queued.

The body is ignored — send `{}`.

delivered.description: Outbox rows claimed across every batch in this pass.

capped.description: The 30-second budget ran out with work still due. A partial pass, not a failure.

No right is required — every screen has to format money before it can draw anything, so an operator who could not read this would read prices in the wrong currency and the wrong number of decimals. Nothing may be added to this payload that is not "what this store is configured as": diagnostics and secrets belong on a route with a right. `notifier_channels` is the one entry here that can be bad news — a channel with no delivery backend sends nothing and reports success — and it belongs anyway, because what it reports is which backends the binary was composed with.

Deliberately not behind `team.write` — that is also the right to change everybody's role, and gating this behind it means a staff member must ask an owner to choose a password for them.

`current_password` is required for either change: a session left open on an unlocked laptop should not be enough to take the account over. Changing the password ends every other session and keeps this one.

An unknown actor_kind, action or entity_type answers with an empty page rather than a 400, because a feed that refuses a stale filter is a screen an operator cannot get out of. It sits behind store.operate: filtering the whole store by person is a different question from the history of one record, which follows that record's own read right.

get.description: Most recently active first, capped at 200. No meta block: it is a short bounded list, and it is built from the trail rather than from the team table.

A record with no rows answers 200 with an empty array rather than 404: the log knowing nothing about a record is not the record being absent, and everything that existed before this table did has an honestly empty history.

Creation, edits and deletion, with parent_id on both sides of a move. A record with no rows answers 200 with an empty array rather than 404: the log knowing nothing about a record is not the record being absent, and everything that existed before this table did has an honestly empty history.

get.summary: Sales totals per day, week or month
get.description: A reading of the orders, added up in the database rather than in the client. A sale is an order whose stock has left the shelf — confirmed, partly shipped, shipped or delivered — so a cash-on-delivery order counts from the moment checkout confirms it, a partly shipped one counts in full, and an in-flight pending checkout that the unpaid sweeper may cancel does not. Pending and cancelled orders are reported beside the totals in `excluded`, never inside them. Payment does not decide whether a sale happened: it splits the same money into `paid`, `outstanding` (pending or failed) and `refunded`, which sum to `total` exactly. Money that has actually gone back is reported rather than netted off — `paid.refunded` for partial refunds, with `paid.net_collected` beside it. `net` is items less discount, and less tax when the prices contained it, so `total = net + tax + shipping` holds under either tax mode. Buckets are calendar day, ISO week (Monday) or month cut in `tz`, and the window's own edges are resolved in that same zone; the first and last bucket carry `partial` when the window clips them. Figures are grouped by the order's own currency and never summed across currencies.

200.description: One block per currency, each with its window totals and its zero-filled buckets.

get.description: The order lines of sales — confirmed, partly shipped, shipped or delivered orders — grouped by product or by variant, within one currency. Title, SKU and variant label are the newest snapshot the lines carry, so a renamed or deleted product still reports under a name somebody recognises; `product_id` is null once the product is gone, and two deleted products stay two rows. `revenue` is line value excluding tax under either tax mode, and BEFORE any order-level discount: a discount is recorded once per order and never allocated to lines, so summing these rows exceeds the sales report's `net` by exactly the discounts in the window.

parameters.name: currency
parameters.description: One ISO code; defaults to the store's configured currency. Ranking across currencies would compare numbers that are not comparable.

200.description: Ranked rows, highest first, with a total tiebreak on the group key so paging never repeats or drops a row.

get.summary: What the outbox has tried to deliver
get.description: A page of `outbox_events`, newest first, behind `store.operate`. The three states partition the table: `published` is `published_at IS NOT NULL`, `dead` is `dead AND published_at IS NULL`, `pending` is the rest — so a row that raced into both flags is counted once, as published. Rows omit `payload`, because a page of order payloads is megabytes and the list is for finding the row rather than reading it; `last_error` is included, because it is what an operator scans the list for. An empty page is `"data": []` and never null.

parameters.name: state
parameters.description: One of the three derived states. Anything else is a 400.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: An exact event name, such as order.paid.

parameters.name: aggregate_type
parameters.description: The kind of thing the event is about, such as order or cart.

parameters.name: aggregate_id
parameters.description: One record's events. Requires aggregate_type: the index is on the pair, and the second column alone is a sequential scan of every event ever delivered.

200.description: A page of the outbox, newest first.

get.description: The row the list found, plus the `payload` the handlers were given. The payload is the event verbatim, so for an order it carries the buyer's email, phone and name and every line they bought — which is why `store.operate` is owner-only by default.

post.description: Two repairs behind one verb, chosen by the row's state under the lock. A **dead** row is un-parked — `dead = false, attempts = 0, available_at = now()` — with a fresh twelve-attempt budget; nothing else can recover it, because the dispatcher's claim filters `NOT dead`. A **pending** row is only brought forward: `available_at = now()`, attempts untouched, because backoff reaches fifteen minutes but the twelve-attempt bound is the whole dead-letter policy and an operator must not be able to hold a broken event in retry forever. A **published** row is refused 409: redelivering a delivered event is a replay, and this engine has no verb for that. Neither act clears `last_error`. No request body is read. The dispatcher is nudged after the commit, so delivery normally follows within milliseconds.

Requeues up to 500 dead letters per call, optionally narrowed to one event name — the same `UPDATE … SET dead = false, attempts = 0` an operator used to run in psql, run by the engine and logged with their name. `remaining` is counted inside the same transaction, so the pair cannot disagree and the panel can say "Retried 500 of 3,214" rather than a bare 500; a non-zero `remaining` means call it again. The claim takes `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, so two operators clearing a backlog take disjoint sets and neither can stall the dispatcher. No request body is read.

An empty rates array is an answer, not an error - this store does not deliver to that destination - and a storefront has to render it either way. A store with no rates configured is still on Config.FlatShippingMinor, and this returns nothing.

post.summary: Price a method inside a zone
post.description: The band is half-open: min_subtotal_minor is inclusive and max_subtotal_minor exclusive, so a Standard at 4900 below 200000 and a Standard at 0 from 200000 are one method the shopper recognises and cannot both claim a basket. Two bands of one name that do overlap are refused, because a shopper offered the same method at two prices has no way to choose.

put.description:
Renumbers a whole sibling set in one transaction, giving the ids sent positions 0..n-1 in the order they arrive. One call rather than a PATCH per row because `position` is per-parent and dense — dropping a row above three siblings renumbers four of them, and separate writes can fail part-way and leave an order that is half old and half new (D54).

`parent_id` is required and nullable: send `null` to reorder the roots. Omitting the key is refused rather than treated as null, so a body that forgets it cannot silently reorder the top level.

`ids` must name exactly that parent's children — all of them, each once, and nothing else. A partial list is refused rather than interpreted, because every reading of one is a guess. Moving a category to a different parent is `parent_id` on PATCH /api/admin/categories/{id}, not this.
